title: NetMoE: Accelerating MoE Training through Dynamic Sample Placement

raw.stage1:
### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to accelerate the all-to-all communication bottleneck in Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) training by introducing a novel perspective: optimizing from the "training sample" viewpoint. This specific framing of the problem — focusing on sample placement to reduce communication overhead — is not explicitly addressed in prior work. While [1], [2], [3], and [9] all aim to mitigate all-to-all communication overhead in MoE training, they do so from different perspectives, such as topology-aware routing ([1]), pipeline parallelism ([2]), overlapping computation and communication ([3]), or general communication efficiency ([9]). None of these papers explicitly approach the problem from the "training sample placement" perspective. Therefore, the purpose is **not covered**.

### Mechanism
The mechanism involves dynamically rearranging sample placement based on expert routing results to align data locality with network locality, converting cross-node communication into intra-node communication or device-internal memory copies without altering computation results. This mechanism is distinct from prior work. While [1] introduces topology-aware routing and [3] overlaps computation and communication, neither employs dynamic sample placement based on expert routing results to optimize communication patterns. Similarly, [9] focuses on accelerating MoE training but does not propose a mechanism equivalent to dynamic sample placement. Other papers, such as [10] and [18], discuss data placement or routing in distributed systems, but their mechanisms are not substantively equivalent to the proposed approach. Thus, the mechanism is **not covered**.

### Evaluation
The evaluation involves training a GPT architecture with all FFN layers replaced by MoE layers on 32 A800 GPUs (4 nodes × 8 GPUs) connected via NVLink and InfiniBand, achieving a 1.67× training efficiency improvement. This evaluation design — measuring training efficiency improvements on a specific hardware setup using a GPT-based MoE model — is **covered** by prior work. For example, [1], [2], [3], and [9] all evaluate MoE training optimizations on distributed GPU clusters, using similar metrics (e.g., training efficiency, communication overhead reduction). While the specific hardware setup and model instance differ, the evaluation design (benchmarking MoE training efficiency improvements on distributed systems) is not novel. Therefore, the evaluation is **covered**.

### Domain
The domain is distributed deep learning, specifically systems for training Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models. This domain is well-established and extensively studied in prior work, including [1], [2], [3], [9], and others. While the contribution targets a specific sub-problem (sample placement optimization) within this domain, it does not introduce a new application area. Thus, the domain is **covered**.
